/-!
# Erdős Problem 63

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/63](https://www.erdosproblems.com/63)
- [dBEr51] de Bruijn, N. G. and Erdős, P., *A colour problem for infinite graphs and a problem
  in the theory of relations*. Indag. Math. (1951), 369--373.
- [ErHa66] Erdős, P. and Hajnal, A., *On chromatic number of graphs and set-systems*.
  Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1966), 61-99.
- [LiMo20] Liu, Hong and Montgomery, Richard, *A solution to Erdős and Hajnal's odd cycle problem*.
  arXiv:2010.15802 (2020).
- [Re24] Reiher, C., *Graphs of large girth*. arXiv:2403.13571 (2024).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos63

/--
Does every graph with infinite chromatic number contain a cycle of length $2^n$ for infinitely
many $n$?

Conjectured by Mihók and Erdős. Solved affirmatively following the work of Liu and Montgomery
[LiMo20].

The linked formal proof (Codex) states the conclusion as `{n | HasCycleLength G (2 ^ n)}.Infinite`,
with `HasCycleLength G m` unfolding to `m ∈ G.cycleLengths`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos63.lean#L46"]
theorem erdos_63 :
    answer(True) ↔
      ∀ {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V), G.chromaticNumber = ⊤ →
        ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n ≥ N, 2 ^ n ∈ G.cycleLengths := by
  sorry

-- TODO: Add variants of the problem.

end Erdos63

reformulations.difference: The source's "graph with infinite chromatic number" is written `G.chromaticNumber = ⊤`, using Mathlib's ℕ∞-valued chromatic number rather than the cardinal-valued `chromaticCardinal`. "For infinitely many n" is written `∀ N : ℕ, ∃ n ≥ N, 2 ^ n ∈ G.cycleLengths`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Mathlib defines `chromaticNumber = ⨅ n ∈ {n | G.Colorable n}, (n : ℕ∞)`, which is ⊤ exactly when G has no proper colouring with finitely many colours (`chromaticNumber_ne_top_iff_exists`). That is exactly "infinite chromatic number". I proved `G.chromaticNumber = ⊤ ↔ ℵ₀ ≤ G.chromaticCardinal` in Lean, for any universe. The problem only needs the finite/infinite split. So the known ℕ∞ limitation (it cannot tell ℵ₁ from ℵ₀, fixed for Erdős 1067/1068 in PR #2011) does not matter here. Graphs of uncountable chromatic number are included. Next, `∀ N, ∃ n ≥ N, P n` is equivalent to `{n | P n}.Infinite` (proved in Lean via `Set.infinite_iff_exists_gt`). This is also exactly the conclusion of the linked formal proof. Finally, `2^n ∈ G.cycleLengths` means G has a cycle walk of length 2^n. For 2^n > 2 this is equivalent to `cycleGraph (2^n) ⊑ G` (Mathlib `cycleGraph_isContained_iff`). Cycle lengths are always ≥ 3, so n = 0, 1 never count.

review.notes:
No findings, because the declaration states the source's question.

Checks:
- The source asks: "Does every graph with infinite chromatic number contain a cycle of length 2^n for infinitely many n?" The page marks it "PROVED (LEAN)", solved in the affirmative.
- The Lean statement elaborates to `Erdos63.erdos_63.{u_1} : True ↔ ∀ {V : Type u_1} (G : SimpleGraph V), G.chromaticNumber = ⊤ → ∀ N, ∃ n ≥ N, 2 ^ n ∈ G.cycleLengths`.
- Every quantifier sits after the answer slot, so the universe problem fixed in PR #4119 does not arise.
- `answer(True)` and `research solved` match the source. There is no status issue.

Lean experiments, all compiled with no errors:
- The right-hand side is equivalent to the linked proof's `Set.Infinite {n | HasCycleLength G (2^n)}` form.
- `chromaticNumber = ⊤ ↔ ∀ n, ¬ G.Colorable n`.
- `chromaticNumber = ⊤ ↔ ℵ₀ ≤ chromaticCardinal`.
- Every cycle length is ≥ 3.
- The hypothesis can be satisfied (the complete graph on ℕ), and 4 is a cycle length of that graph.

The formal_proof record is consistent:
- The link resolves to the theorem at L46 of the pinned commit.
- Its statement implies, and in fact is equivalent to, the repository statement.
- I could not build the external project (Lean v4.33.0) to run `#print axioms`.
- A text scan of the 42 Erdos63 supporting modules and Erdos760.lean found no `sorry`, `axiom` or `native_decide`.
- erdosproblems.com itself records the Lean verification.

The source remarks that 2^n can likely be replaced by any sufficiently fast-growing sequence, such as the squares. The file only has a TODO for variants. A missing variant is not a defect.

The docstring's third paragraph is a note about the formal proof. It is accurate, but it is closer to a review note than a problem statement. This is a style point only.
